rv.q: The autobiographical narrative, accompanied by carefully edited home videos, is both funny and often deeply moving.
It aims to please, and succeeds.
A charming work that strikes a deep chord … It's a joyful love letter to self-expression.

Luke Sheppard’s production, meanwhile, in which ordinary living-room furniture is magically transformed – like a chest of drawers becoming a cascading staircase, or spotlights hidden in a cupboard – captures the sheer elation of creativity.
It may not dig very deep, but the audience whooped, screamed and shouted.
By the end of the magical show, one feels emotionally lifted in ways that theatre often struggles to accomplish.
An inspiring, poignant and joyous celebration of life beyond the binary, this show affirms the unconditional support of parents and carers who really do love their own, no matter what.
It’s a delightful and magical transformation on which to end the show.
My Son’s a Queer recounts a near-blessed upbringing, all but demanding that Madge’s family take its own richly deserved bow.
It’s an authentic, feel-good fairy-tale come true: Rob’s story really is one to celebrate.
Everything about this show just works.

cn.t: Critics praise this heartwarming, uplifting solo show for its charm and emotional resonance, though some find it slight or underwritten. Madge's nostalgic home videos and celebration of supportive parenting win hearts in this joyful, feel-good production.
